fields.AN_Notes: Conceptual paper mapping Long and Magerko's AI literacy framework onto the nine CSWE core competencies. Bias axes come from the authors' own worked examples: a mortgage denial that ignores informal income (Socioeconomic) and a mental-health agency model trained on English-speaking insured clients (Language_Culture, Socioeconomic); race and disability appear only in enumerations and cited cases. Harm types: the lending example is an allocation in which an apparently neutral criterion disadvantages the family (Indirect_Discrimination); the agency example makes the dominant client group the default and overlooks marginalised groups (Exclusionary_Norms). Mitigation is recommended only: advocacy for more inclusive data (Pre_Processing) and human review, appeals, community forums, training and governance (Organisational_Process). Tasks are named as AI uses in practice: summarising case histories and drafting reports, risk and needs identification, chatbots and drafting client communication, scheduling and data entry, research uses of LLMs, classroom use. The AI literacy framework frames competencies, not the treatment of bias, so AN_Theory_Reference is No; 'antiracist and intersectional lenses' appear only as a recommendation in Table 2.

fields.AN_Notes: Case-study based argument for a technical-critical social work pedagogy on ADM (AFST, COMPAS, NDIS, HEALER, Heat List). fields.AN_Notes: Technofeminist chapter on the gender relations of AI: women's under-representation in AI and data science (including the authors' own platform analysis), masculinity and technical expertise, and the feedback loop into biased systems. Race_Ethnicity and Intersectional follow the authors' own argument that women of colour are particularly under-represented and that gender intersects with race and class; listed cases of discriminatory systems (Amazon hiring, chatbot hate speech, mask recognition, pulse oximetry, Gender Shades) are cited only and do not ground harm codes. Exclusionary_Norms: masculine defaults and masculine preferences inscribed in AI; Erasure: under-representation of groups in training data and the gender data gap, argued as the chapter's own feedback-loop mechanism. Mitigation: more diverse teams, recruitment practices, leadership and more nuanced data on women in AI are proposed; university initiatives that raised women's share in computer science are reported as workforce interventions, not as evaluated bias mitigations, so Proposed. Technical fairness metrics are criticised as insufficient.

fields.AN_Notes: Narrative review of AI in social sciences and social work 2022 to 2025. The synthesis has its own section 'Algorithmic Discrimination and Bias' and case-study section; axes coded from these: race (COMPAS) and low income (child-welfare flagging, Robodebt). Disability and single mothers appear in one sentence on French welfare litigation only. Indirect_Discrimination: allocation decisions (child-welfare flagging, debt notices, risk scores) that disadvantage groups through historical training data and data matching, without the group attribute as decision criterion; the work does not itself classify direct or indirect. Mitigation: diverse training datasets (Pre_Processing), adversarial debiasing and fairness constraints (In_Training), human oversight, bias audits and collaborative governance (Organisational_Process); the review reports these as implemented in pilot programmes without a reported result, hence Demonstrated. Source-quality note: several references carry placeholder URLs ('xxxx') and implausible bibliographic data, flagged for the domain experts; codes rely only on the work's own statements.

fields.AN_Notes: Survey and taxonomy of intersectional fairness notions (subgroup, calibration-based, metric-based, differential, max-min, probabilistic) and mitigation (with and without demographics), plus NLP, ranking and auditing applications. Bias axes structure the synthesis through intersectional groups of gender and race (e.g. Black women); disability, socioeconomic status and others appear only in reported studies. Harm types structure the synthesis as fairness notions: outcome parity in decisions with the disparate-impact four-fifths rule extended by differential fairness (Indirect_Discrimination) and worst-case accuracy or loss across subgroups (Disparate_Performance). Mitigation stages synthesised: in-processing (DRO, adversarial reweighting, auditor-learner game), post-processing (multicalibration boosting, multiaccuracy post-processing, prediction flipping) and stakeholder involvement and auditing (Organisational_Process). Evaluated refers to synthesised experimental results of the reviewed methods (adversarial reweighting and Pareto approaches improve fairness for some intersectional groups; independent-group debiasing prone to gerrymandering), not to an experiment of the survey itself. Feministisch ja rests on Crenshaw's intersectionality as the frame of the whole survey.
